## Sealed comparison (U57, U58) - Purpose: compare several published arms on one box under a design fixed before the run. Owner approval 2026-11-03 (contract gaps G1 comparison arms, G3 tolerance and equivalence, G6 compute metadata of the blind-02 science route); requirements from science steps s13 to s23. Arms are published programs or configurations that need no new code, run by the pipeline from sealed argument vectors. Each invocation runs one arm on one input, and invocations are interleaved on one box. No agent computes a number: every number comes from the pipeline's trusted wall time, from rules fixed before the run and applied by the pipeline, from a trusted comparator of two arms' outputs, or from a published evaluator that runs on each arm's output without access to the arm's identity. Criteria, margins, thresholds, reference values and timeouts are fixed by a science step before the run, sealed, and unreadable by the run's agents and by the processes of arms and evaluator. Compute is recorded twice and never mixed: per invocation as attribution and per box allocation as the bill. Never change a criterion after a result: every decision uses the sealed design. An outcome that is not supported is a result and never fails a stage. Comparisons that need more than one run are split by the science step into one design per run; a design whose launch depends on an earlier run's outcomes is launched only when the science step finds them in that run's `C/comparison_scored.json`. Without `args.comparison`, every stage is unchanged. Declared residual risks, which no rule below removes: the evaluator reads the arm's output files by design, so file names or content under `out/` that identify the program can reach it (the sealed `evaluate.sh` bytes make any dependence on them auditable after the run); state of shared hardware (device memory, caches, timing) is not cleared between parts; a harness script that disobeys the rule that only `fetch_private.sh` handles the evaluator's private data can leave a transformed copy of them (an archive, a re-encoding, a derived file) where the arm part can read it, which the byte-identity check of Separated users step 7 does not detect (`setup.sh` and its repairs are kept in `A/harness/` and the stage's receipts, so such a copy is auditable after the run); and processes, shell start-up hooks or scheduled jobs that `setup.sh`, its repairs or the anchors leave behind run as the box user, which the pipeline's own box commands also use, so they can read and change what the box user can (the same kept bytes make them auditable; the hash check of Separated users step 1 detects a sealed harness file changed before it). - Optional `args.comparison` is an object with exactly the key `design`: a non-empty path, resolved relative to the pipeline working directory, to a design JSON file. It is exclusive with `args.card`, `args.units_check` and `args.units_probe`. The design is exactly `{arms, inputs, outputs, metrics, evaluator, replicates, warmup, order_seed, timeout_s, budget_s, bootstrap_seed, bootstrap_resamples, comparisons}`: - `arms`: 2 to 5 items, each exactly `{id, what, commands, env}`; ids `"A0"`, `"A1"`, ... in order; `what` a non-empty string. `A0` is the published baseline that intake and reproduce handle as usual. - `commands`: 1 to 8 commands, each a non-empty array of non-empty strings: the exact published command lines of the arm, in order, as argument vectors run without a shell. The pipeline runs them (see Evaluate); the arm's adapter only prepares. - `env`: null or an object mapping names that match `^[A-Z_][A-Z0-9_]{0,63}$` and do not start with `CMP_` to strings; set for the arm's commands. - Placeholders, in command and `env` strings only: `{input}` (the input id), `{run}`, `{out}` (the absolute paths of the invocation's `run/` and `out/`) and `{spec:

}` with `

` a JSON Pointer (RFC 6901) into the input's `spec`, which must resolve in every input's `spec` to a string (inserted as is) or a finite number (inserted as `json.dumps` writes it). `{{` and `}}` stand for literal braces; any other `{` or `}` makes the design invalid. Substitution replaces every occurrence and is not repeated on its result. - `inputs`: 1 to 10 items, each exactly `{id, spec}`: `id` a unique string matching `^[A-Za-z0-9][A-Za-z0-9._-]{0,63}$`; `spec` any JSON value (pins, case, configuration). - `outputs`: 0 to 10 items, each exactly `{name, what, format, select}`: a logical result each arm, or the evaluator, writes for an input, compared across arms. `name` unique, matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,30}$`; `what` a non-empty string; `format` `"bytes"`, `"text_numbers"` (every number in the file's UTF-8 text, in order, as matched by `[-+]?(\d+\.?\d*|\.\d+)([eE][-+]?\d+)?` together with `nan`, `inf` and `-inf` tokens) or `"json_numbers"` (every number leaf of the JSON document, in document order; booleans are not numbers). `select` is null (the whole content) or, for `bytes` and `text_numbers` only, a Python `re` pattern with at least one capturing group: the content is read as UTF-8 with replacement, and the selected content is every group of every match of `re.finditer(select, text, re.MULTILINE)`, in order (an unmatched group as the empty string), joined by `"\n"`; `format` then applies to the selected content (`bytes` to its UTF-8 encoding). Several outputs may select different parts of the same file, each with its own comparison and tolerance. - `metrics`: 1 to 10 items, each exactly `{name, unit, what, source, reduce, expect_count}`: `name` unique, matching `^[a-z][a-z0-9_]{0,30}$`; `unit` and `what` non-empty strings; `source` `"trusted_wall"` or `"sealed_extraction"`. - `trusted_wall`: the invocation's wall seconds: the adapter's wall plus its commands' walls, plus the evaluator's wall when the design has an evaluator. `reduce` and `expect_count` are null. - `sealed_extraction`: read from fetched files by a rule the harness agent fixes before the run, reduced as the design states. `reduce` `"first"`, `"max"` or `"value_at_max_key"`; `expect_count` null or a positive integer, the number of matched values the rule must find. - `evaluator`: null or exactly `{what, spec, timeout_s}`: a published, pinned program that reads one arm's output for one input, with data that only it may read, and writes evaluation files. `what` a non-empty string; `spec` any JSON value (program, pin, command, and where its private data come from); `timeout_s` null or a positive integer. - `replicates` an integer from 1 to 30; `warmup` an integer from 0 to 3; `order_seed` and `bootstrap_seed` integers; `bootstrap_resamples` an integer from 1000 to 1000000; `budget_s` a positive integer, the evaluate stage's time budget for this comparison. When `args.run_ceiling_s` is present, `budget_s` must be below it. - `timeout_s`: null, a positive integer for every invocation, or an object mapping every arm id to a positive integer or to an object mapping every input id to a positive integer: the cap of one invocation's arm part. - `comparisons`: 0 to 12 items (0: a run that only records values and compute, for example to derive later reference values), each exactly `{id, arm, against, measure, criterion, direction, unit, pairing, rule, confidence, margin, threshold, strict, reference, missing, given, parts}`: - `id` unique, matching `^K[0-9]{1,2}$`; `arm` an arm id; `against` a different arm id or `"reference"`; `parts` a non-empty array of unique non-empty strings. - `measure` is exactly `{metric}` (a metric name) or exactly `{output, comparator}` (an output name and one of `"exact"`, `"elementwise_abs"`, `"elementwise_abs_plus_rel_max"`). An output comparison needs an arm as `against`. - `criterion` `"agreement"` (every output comparison and no metric comparison), `"non_inferiority"`, `"superiority"` or `"ratio_at_least"`. - `direction` `"higher_better"`, `"lower_better"` or `"two_sided"`: the metric as measured (for wall seconds, `lower_better`). `agreement` and `superiority` use `two_sided`; `non_inferiority` and `ratio_at_least` use `higher_better` or `lower_better`. - `unit` `"pooled_mean"` (each replicate's value is the mean over inputs, decided once), `"per_input_all"` (decided per input; the comparison holds only if it holds on every input) or `"per_input_each"` (decided and reported per input). - `pairing` `"paired_replicate"` or `"unpaired"`; `rule` `"all_pairs"` or `"bootstrap"`; `confidence` a number in `[0.5, 1)` for `bootstrap` and null for `all_pairs`. `ratio_at_least` uses exactly `pooled_mean`, `paired_replicate` and `bootstrap`; every other criterion uses `all_pairs` and a per-input unit; agreement uses `paired_replicate`. - `margin`: for an output comparison, the comparator's tolerance: null for `exact`, `{"abs": x}` for `elementwise_abs`, `{"abs": x, "rel": y}` for `elementwise_abs_plus_rel_max`. For `non_inferiority` and `superiority`, null or `{"abs": x}`. For `ratio_at_least`, null. `x` and `y` are finite and nonnegative. - `threshold`: a finite number above 0 for `ratio_at_least`, otherwise null. `strict`: a boolean for `ratio_at_least` (true: the bound must exceed `threshold`; false: it may equal it), otherwise null. - `reference`: exactly when `against` is `"reference"`, an object `{source, values}`: `source` a non-empty string naming where the values come from (for example an earlier run of this route and the rule that derived them), `values` mapping every input id to a finite number; otherwise null. A reference needs a metric `measure`, a per-input unit and `unpaired`. - `missing`: `"void"` or `"fail"`, how a missing value is decided (see Scoring). - `given`: an array, possibly empty, of unique ids of comparisons that come earlier in `comparisons`; a decision unit is decided only when each of them is supported for it (see Scoring). An invalid argument or design, or a path that cannot be read as JSON, fails intake with `error_class: parse` before any agent call. - Before the intake agent call and any box command, the pipeline writes atomically, in this order: `C/comparison.json`, exactly `{source, source_sha256, design}`; `C/comparison_seal.json`, exactly `{comparison_sha256, sealed_utc}` (the SHA-256 of the exact bytes of `C/comparison.json`); and `A/comparison_view.json`, exactly `{arms, inputs, outputs, metrics, evaluator, replicates, warmup}` copied from the design, with `evaluator` reduced to `{what, spec}` (null when the design's is null). The view holds no comparison, criterion, margin, threshold, reference value, timeout, part, seed or budget. Agents see only the view; comparison-mode prompts name it and never `C/` or the design path. The run root, the workflow journal directory and the design file must lie outside the pipeline working directory, which the isolation runner exposes to every agent call; otherwise intake fails with `error_class: parse` before any agent call. The science step that writes the design is responsible for the view's free text (`what`, `spec`, `select`) stating no expectation, criterion or result, and for keeping no copy of the design on the pipeline host outside the paths hidden below. - Isolation of agent calls, comparison mode only. Every agent call of the run (intake, harness, and every setup and anchors repair) is dispatched with wf `isolation` (see Implement) as implement's calls are: `directory` a fresh private view created for that call under the system temporary directory, `box_access` false, and `hidden` holding the run root, the workflow journal directory, the design file's parent directory and, when the design file lies inside a git work tree, that work tree's top-level directory (the nearest ancestor that contains `.git`). Under `isolation` the rest of the host is read-only and the view is the only writable host directory, so each role gets copies of what it reads today and writes only into its view; the pipeline copies its results back: - intake view: `comparison_view.json`; when the brief is a file, `brief/` (a copy of its bytes), which the prompt names in place of the brief's path; and an empty `intake/`. After the call the pipeline copies each regular file directly under the view's `intake/` (no symbolic link, no subdirectory) to `A/intake/`. - harness view: `comparison_view.json`, `intake/` (a copy of `A/intake/`) and an empty `harness/`; the probe stays in the prompt as today. After the call the pipeline copies each regular file directly under the view's `harness/`, and each regular file `harness/arms/.sh`, to the same name under `A/harness/`. - setup or anchors repair view: `comparison_view.json`, `intake/` and `harness/` (copies of `A/intake/` and `A/harness/`); the probe and log tail stay in the prompt. After the call the pipeline copies back only the scripts that repair may rewrite today (`setup.sh`; or `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh`), and discards every other change, as the existing restore of protected scripts does. When the view's `intake/`, `harness/` or `harness/arms/` is not a directory (a symbolic link included), nothing is copied from it, and no copy follows a symbolic link. Prompts name the view's paths in place of `A/intake/` and `A/harness/`. Network access is unchanged by `isolation`. A call that cannot be dispatched so fails as an isolation failure does; there is no fallback. Views are removed after the stage. - Intake prompt, comparison mode only: the run compares the view's arms on the view's inputs; `A0` is the benchmark intake records as usual; intake also records, in `benchmark.json` under the key `arms`, each other arm's published source, pin and commands, under the key `evaluator` the evaluator's published source, pin and command when the view has one, and in `data.json` every input any arm or the evaluator needs, marking the evaluator's private data and stating where each private item is published. - Harness prompt, comparison mode only: `setup.sh` also builds or installs every arm's published program and configuration, and the evaluator, as published, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. `setup.sh` never fetches, copies or writes the evaluator's private data; only `fetch_private.sh` does (see Separated users). The harness agent writes, besides the usual scripts: - one adapter `harness/arms/.sh` per arm, `A0` included, which only prepares the invocation (stages the input named by `CMP_INPUT` under `run/` or `CMP_OUT`) and never runs the arm's program, writes or patches source, or computes, writes or asserts a metric; - when the view has an evaluator, `harness/fetch_private.sh`, which fetches every input `data.json` marks as the evaluator's private data from where it is published, writing only under its working directory, and `harness/evaluate.sh`, which runs the published, pinned evaluator on the arm output in `CMP_ARM_OUT` for the input named by `CMP_INPUT`, reads private data only under `CMP_PRIVATE`, writes its results under `CMP_EVAL_OUT`, and never writes elsewhere; - `harness/cmp_files.json`, exactly `{"files": {...}}`, mapping each arm id to an object that maps every output name to a location: a relative path, or exactly `{glob}` with `glob` a pattern of relative-path components that may also use `*`, `?`, `[` and `]`. Locations are relative to the invocation directory, and their first component is `out` (the arm's files), `log` (the standard output and error of the arm's adapter and commands) or `eval` (the evaluator's files); - `harness/cmp_extract.json`, exactly `{"rules": [...]}`, one rule per arm and `sealed_extraction` metric, each exactly `{arm, metric, file, kind, expr}`, with `file` a relative path whose first component is `out`, `log` or `eval`, and `kind` and `expr` as defined for `harness/card_extract.json` (U54), extended by the metric's `reduce`: `kind` `"json"`: `expr` points to a finite number, to an array of finite numbers, or (for `value_at_max_key`) to an array of two-element arrays `[key, value]` of finite numbers; `kind` `"regex"`: exactly one capturing group, or exactly two (key, then value) for `value_at_max_key`; - `harness/versions.sh`, which prints one JSON object mapping each arm id, and `"evaluator"` when the view has one, to exactly `{version, executable}`: the program's version string and the path, absolute or relative to the shared run directory, of its main executable file. Relative paths are one or more `/`-separated components made of `[A-Za-z0-9._+=-]`, none `.` or `..`. `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh` keep their meaning for `A0`. - After harness generation or copy (with `args.harness_from`, the source directory must also hold `arms/`, `cmp_files.json`, `cmp_extract.json`, `versions.sh` and, when the design has an evaluator, `fetch_private.sh` and `evaluate.sh`, copied like the scripts) and before the harness upload, those files must exist and be valid: `harness/arms/` holds exactly one non-empty adapter per arm; `fetch_private.sh` and `evaluate.sh` exist exactly when the design has an evaluator; `cmp_files.json` maps every arm and every output, with `eval` locations only when the design has an evaluator; and `cmp_extract.json` has exactly one rule per arm and `sealed_extraction` metric, whose group count matches the metric's `reduce`. Otherwise reproduce fails with `error_class: parse` before the upload. The pipeline then writes `C/arms_seal.json`, exactly `{files, sealed_utc}`, mapping each of those files' names (adapters as `arms/.sh`) to the SHA-256 of its bytes. They upload with the harness, in the same encoding. No repair changes them. - In comparison mode, a probe whose `sudo_nopasswd` is not true fails reproduce with `error_class: infra` right after the probe, before the harness call: the separated users below need it. The rule that harness scripts use sudo only for apt is unchanged; only the pipeline's trusted scripts below use it otherwise. - In comparison mode reproduce runs exactly as usual for `A0`. Profile, seal, propose and implement are SKIPPED. Evaluate runs the comparison when reproduce passed, and is SKIPPED otherwise, as after any failed gate. - Evaluate, comparison mode (U57): - Separated users, for every comparison (`cmp-eval`, `cmp-private` and steps 5 to 7 only when the design has an evaluator): one box command, operation `comparison-users`, runs the trusted `bash profiler/cmp_users.sh` (written inline by the pipeline). With `sudo -n`, in this order, it: 1. checks that every file `C/arms_seal.json` names has, under the shared run directory's `harness/`, the SHA-256 sealed there (the pipeline writes the expected values into the script), and fails otherwise; then creates, when absent, the system users without login shell or home, `cmp-arm` and, with an evaluator, `cmp-eval` (the part users), and adds them to every group that owns a `/dev/nvidia*` device file whose permission bits for other users lack read or write; adds each part user to `/etc/cron.deny` and `/etc/at.deny` (creating either when absent) and removes it from `/etc/cron.allow` and `/etc/at.allow` when either exists (an allow list takes precedence over its deny list), so that no part user can schedule a job; 2. rejects every outgoing packet of `cmp-arm` except on the loopback interface, with an owner-match rule in both `iptables` and `ip6tables`; 3. recursively removes group and other write access from the shared run directory and grants other users read access to every file, execute access to every file that any user may execute, and search access to every directory in it (the effect of `chmod -R go-w,o+rX`), except `cmp-private` and the evaluate stage's own box command files (top-level files named `NNNN-.sh|log|gpu|rc` as `m5/boxrun.sh` names them, at mode `600`; see Remote command files), which keep their mode; creates `comparison-work/` and `comparison-jobs/` owned by the box user at modes `711` and `700`; and, with an evaluator, creates `cmp-private` empty (removing any earlier one), owned by `cmp-eval` at mode `700`; 4. writes `profiler/cmp_writable.json`, mapping each part user to the sorted list of directories outside the shared run directory it can write, as printed by `sudo -n -u find / \( -path /proc -o -path /sys -o -path \) -prune -o -type d -writable -print`; 5. with an evaluator, runs `bash /harness/fetch_private.sh` as `cmp-eval` (as a part runs, below) with working directory `cmp-private` and `HOME` and `TMPDIR` set to `cmp-private/.home` (created empty, removed afterwards), then cleans up after `cmp-eval` (below); a nonzero exit fails; 6. with an evaluator, fails when `cmp-private` holds anything other than regular files and directories, and otherwise makes it and everything under it owned by `root` with group `cmp-eval`, with directories at mode `750` and files at mode `640`, so the evaluator can read and never change it; 7. with an evaluator, fails when any regular file outside `cmp-private` that lies in the shared run directory, under the box user's home directory, or below a directory listed for `cmp-arm` in `profiler/cmp_writable.json` has the size and SHA-256 of a regular file under `cmp-private`; 8. checks that `sudo -n -u nvidia-smi -L` prints, for each part user, the same number of GPU lines as for the box user, that `sudo -n -u cmp-arm test -r cmp-private` fails (with an evaluator), and that the two rules of step 2 are present (`iptables -C`, `ip6tables -C`). Any failure fails evaluate with `error_class: infra` before any invocation. Cleanup after a part user runs with `sudo -n` and never deletes or changes anything in the shared run directory: entries there are handled only by the explicit rules for `cmp-private` (steps 5-6) and for invocation directories (wrapper steps 2-4). It is: first remove the user's crontab and every at job of the user (`crontab -r -u `, and `atrm` for each job `atq` lists for the user, each only when that tool is installed), so that no job of the user starts after its processes are killed; then kill every process of the user (`pkill -KILL -u `) once per second until `pgrep -u ` finds none, for at most the time left in `budget_s`; for each directory `

` listed for the user in `profiler/cmp_writable.json` that is not below another listed directory, delete every entry the user owns below it outside the shared run directory, `find -mindepth 1 -user ! -path ! -path /* -delete`, with `` the shared run directory's absolute path, each `*`, `?`, `[` and `\` in it escaped by a backslash, and each pattern passed as one argument (an exclusion by `-path`, because `-delete` implies `-depth` and so voids `-prune`); and remove every System V IPC object the user owns. The arm part therefore cannot read the evaluator's private data or anything the evaluator left behind, cannot reach the network, cannot write any file the evaluator or the wrapper runs, and cannot change modes that protect them, whatever its adapter or commands do. - Versions: one box command, operation `versions`, runs `bash harness/versions.sh` with stdout to `out/comparison/versions.json`, then the trusted `python3 profiler/cmp_system.py` (written inline by the pipeline) writes `out/comparison/system.json`, exactly `{cpu_model, cpu_logical, kernel, driver_version, cuda_version, gpus, executables}`: `lscpu` model name and logical CPU count; `uname -r`; the driver and CUDA versions that `nvidia-smi` reports; `gpus` one row per GPU, exactly `{index, name, uuid, memory_total}`, from `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,uuid,memory.total --format=csv,noheader`; and `executables` mapping each key of `versions.json` to exactly `{version, executable, sha256, libraries}`, with `sha256` the SHA-256 of the executable's resolved file and `libraries` one row per `ldd` line of the form ` => ...`, exactly `{name, path, sha256}` (the resolved file's SHA-256), or `[]` when `ldd` fails or reports a static executable. Any field that cannot be read is null. - Rounds: `warmup` warmup rounds, then `replicates` replicate rounds. Each round runs every (arm, input) pair once, in an order drawn from one `random.Random(order_seed)` stream: one `shuffle` of the round's pairs per round, warmups included. Invocation `k` (from 1, in run order, warmups included) has the token `i`, which names it on the box; no box path, file name, process argument or environment variable that the evaluator part can read names the arm. - Each invocation is two box commands from the shared run directory. First, operation `comparison-job` writes the job file `comparison-jobs/i.json`, exactly `{arm, input, mode, round, arm_timeout_s, eval_timeout_s, left_s}` (mode `warmup` or `replicate`; the timeouts resolved as under Timeouts when this command starts; `left_s` the smaller of the time left in `budget_s` and the time left before the run ceiling then, in seconds), in the harness upload encoding, at mode `600`, owned by the box user. Second, operation `comparison` runs the trusted wrapper `python3 profiler/cmp_wrap.py i` (written inline by the pipeline, as the profile stage writes its probe), whose only argument is the token. The wrapper reads its job file and builds a fresh invocation directory `comparison-work/i/` at mode `711`, holding `run/` (a symbolic link to every top-level entry of the shared run directory except `out`, `profiler`, `concurrency-work`, `evaluation-work`, `units-check`, `comparison-work`, `comparison-jobs` and `cmp-private`), an empty `out/`, an empty `log/` at mode `700` owned by the box user, an empty `eval/`, and empty `home/` and `ehome/`. The part user is `cmp-arm` for the arm part and `cmp-eval` for the evaluator part. `run/`, `out/` and `home/` are owned by `cmp-arm`, and `eval/` and `ehome/` by `cmp-eval`. A part runs as `sudo -n -u -- env -i `; its variables are the wrapper's environment without any `CMP_`, `SUDO_` or `HOME` name, with `HOME` set to `home/` (arm part) or `ehome/` (evaluator part), plus the part's `CMP_` variables below. The wrapper opens every log file itself and passes it to the part as standard output or error. The wrapper: 1. arm part: runs `bash harness/arms/.sh` with working directory `run/`, with standard output and error written to `log/adapter.stdout` and `log/adapter.stderr`; then, when the adapter exits 0, runs each of the arm's commands in order with working directory `run/`, after placeholder substitution and with the arm's `env`, with standard output and error written to `log/cmd.stdout` and `log/cmd.stderr` (`k` from 1), stopping at the first nonzero exit. A first argument containing `/` resolves relative to `run/`, otherwise through `PATH`. Its variables are `CMP_INPUT` (the input id), `CMP_INPUT_SPEC` (the JSON of that input's `spec`) and `CMP_OUT` (the absolute path of `out/`); 2. after the arm part: cleans up after `cmp-arm` (see Separated users; processes still left make the invocation `invalid`); removes `home/`; makes `run/` and `out/` and everything under them owned by the box user, restores owner read, write and search access to everything under `out/` (the effect of `chmod -R u+rwX`), and sets `run/` to mode `700`; makes the invocation `invalid` when any of this fails or when `out/` holds anything other than regular files and directories (a symbolic link included); then removes group and other write access and grants other users read and search access under `out/`; 3. evaluator part, only when the design has an evaluator and the arm part's status is `ok`: runs `bash /harness/evaluate.sh` with the shared run directory as working directory and the variables `CMP_INPUT`, `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`, `CMP_ARM_OUT` (the absolute path of `out/`), `CMP_EVAL_OUT` (the absolute path of `eval/`) and `CMP_PRIVATE` (the absolute path of `cmp-private`); then cleans up after `cmp-eval` as in step 2, removes `ehome/`, and makes `eval/` and everything under it owned by the box user; 4. sets the invocation directory to mode `700`, so that no later part reads this invocation's files, then writes `wrap.json` in it, atomically and last, at mode `600`, exactly `{status, adapter_rc, adapter_wall_s, commands, gpu_busy_s, gpu_busy_known, eval_status, eval_rc, eval_wall_s, eval_gpu_busy_s, eval_gpu_busy_known}`. `status` is `"ok"` (the adapter and every command exited 0), `"failed"` (a nonzero exit), `"timeout"` or `"invalid"`; `commands` has one row per command started, exactly `{argv, rc, wall_s, executable, sha256}` (the substituted argument vector, exit status, `perf_counter` wall seconds, the resolved executable path and its SHA-256, null when unresolved); `eval_status` is `"ok"`, `"failed"`, `"timeout"` or `"skipped"` (no evaluator, or the arm part was not `ok`). Walls are `perf_counter` seconds and exit statuses null on timeout. GPU-busy seconds are sampled separately for the arm part and the evaluator part (`nvidia-smi --query-gpu=utilization.gpu` immediately and every second; each finite sample in [0,100] contributes `utilization / 100` seconds, summed over GPUs; the matching `known` flag is false when no valid sample was taken). The invocation's `out/`, `log/`, `eval/` and `wrap.json` are fetched to `A/results/evaluate/comparison/ or r>///` (`r` the round index), from the pipeline's own record of each token's job. - Remote command files: every box command of the evaluate stage in comparison mode creates its own files on the box (the command script, log, GPU samples and exit status that `m5/boxrun.sh` writes) at mode `600` before writing to them, so no part user reads a job's contents. - After the last invocation, with an evaluator, one box command, operation `comparison-private-remove`, removes `cmp-private` with `sudo -n rm -rf`; its outcome is recorded in the stage's receipts and changes no value or outcome. - Timeouts: the arm part's timeout is the smallest of its `timeout_s` (when non-null), the time left in `budget_s`, and the time left before the run ceiling; the evaluator part's is the smallest of `evaluator.timeout_s` (when non-null) and the same two. The wrapper further caps each part's timeout by `left_s` minus the seconds elapsed since the wrapper started; when that is below 1 s when the evaluator part would start, the evaluator part is not run and `eval_status` is `"timeout"` with `eval_rc` and `eval_wall_s` null. On a timeout the wrapper kills every process of the part user, as in cleanup, and records `"timeout"`. When the time left in `budget_s` is below 1 s, the remaining invocations are not run, and their status is `"not_run"`. A missing or invalid `wrap.json` gives status `"invalid"`: it is invalid unless it has exactly the keys above with their types (walls and GPU-busy seconds finite and nonnegative or null as stated, exit statuses integers or null, `commands` rows exactly as stated), `status` is `"ok"` exactly when `adapter_rc` and every command's `rc` are 0 and the arm has as many command rows as commands, and `eval_status` is `"ok"` only when `eval_rc` is 0. - Values: for an invocation with status `ok`, a `trusted_wall` metric is `adapter_wall_s` plus its commands' `wall_s`, plus `eval_wall_s` when the design has an evaluator (null unless `eval_status` is `ok`). A `sealed_extraction` metric is its rule applied to the fetched file: the matched values are every `float()`-parsed match of the regex in order, or the number or array at the pointer. With `reduce` `first` or `max`, the value is that function of the matched values; with `value_at_max_key`, it is the value of the first pair whose key is the largest. A file under `eval` needs `eval_status` `ok`. A missing or unreadable file, no match, a nonfinite matched number, or a match count other than a non-null `expect_count` gives null. Every value of an invocation with any other status is null. A null value is a missing value. - Compute (G6): `A/results/evaluate/comparison_compute.json`, written atomically after the last invocation, is exactly `{invocations, arms, all_invocations, system, versions, allocation}`. - `invocations` has one row per scheduled invocation in run order, each exactly `{round, arm, input, status, wall_s, gpu_busy_s, gpu_busy_known, eval_status, eval_wall_s, eval_gpu_busy_s, attributed_usd}`, from `wrap.json`: `wall_s` is `adapter_wall_s` plus the commands' walls, and `attributed_usd` is `(wall_s + eval_wall_s) / 3600 * C/box.json.price_usd_h`, with a null wall counted as 0 and null when the price is unavailable. Rows of `not_run` invocations have null numbers. - `arms` has one row per arm, each exactly `{arm, invocations, wall_s, gpu_busy_s, gpu_busy_known, eval_wall_s, eval_gpu_busy_s, attributed_usd}`, summed over that arm's replicate invocations whatever their status, with a null counted as 0; `gpu_busy_known` is true only when every summed row's flag is. - `all_invocations` is exactly `{invocations, wall_s, eval_wall_s, attributed_usd}`, summed over every row, warmups and failures included, with a null counted as 0. - `system` and `versions` copy the fetched `system.json` and `versions.json` (null when missing or invalid). - `allocation` is the bill of the whole box allocation, which may include work outside this run, exactly `{type, price_usd_h, started_utc, ended_utc, hours, usd, final}` from `C/box.json`. When that record has `ended_utc` and `hours`, they are copied and `final` is true; otherwise `ended_utc` is null, `hours` is the time from `started_utc` to when the file is written, and `final` is false. `usd` is `hours * price_usd_h`. Unavailable fields are null. At takeaways, after a matching allocation record refreshes `C/box.json` (see Compute metadata), the pipeline rewrites the file atomically with only `allocation` recomputed. The run's own share stays `run_box_usd`. Uploads, links, job files, user setup, the private-data fetch and removal, cleanups and fetches are outside every invocation row; they remain in the stage's receipts. - Scoring (U58): after the last invocation, `python3 -I m5/score_comparison.py `. It checks the SHA-256 of `C/comparison.json` against `C/comparison_seal.json` and of each sealed harness file against `C/arms_seal.json`, then scores each comparison, in design order, from the replicate rounds only. - Locations: a relative path names one file. A `{glob}` location names the regular files that Python `glob.glob(glob, root_dir=)` returns, sorted by a key that splits the relative path into runs of digits and non-digits, compares digit runs as integers and breaks ties by the path; their contents, each after `select`, are joined by `"\n"` (by `b"\n"` for `bytes`). A side of an (input, replicate) pair is missing when its invocation's status is not `ok`, when the location is under `eval` and `eval_status` is not `ok`, when the location names no file or an unreadable one, when the content cannot be parsed as the output's `format`, or when the selected content is empty (no bytes for `bytes`, no numbers otherwise). - Output comparisons (`agreement`): for each input and replicate where neither side is missing, the comparator compares the two contents. `exact`: identical bytes. Otherwise both contents are parsed as the output's `format` into number lists; different lengths, or a NaN in one list but not at the same position in the other, disagree; equal infinities agree; finite pairs agree when `abs(a - b) <= abs_tol` (`elementwise_abs`) or `abs(a - b) <= abs_tol + rel_tol * max(abs(a), abs(b))` (`elementwise_abs_plus_rel_max`). A pair agrees when every element agrees. Each compared pair records `max_abs_error` and `max_rel_error` over its finite elements (null when none). - Metric comparisons: an arm's value for (replicate, input) is the metric value above. For `pooled_mean`, a replicate's value is the mean over inputs, null when any input's value is null. Per decision unit (the pooled value, or each input): for `paired_replicate`, the differences are `arm - against` per replicate; for `unpaired`, the differences of every arm value with every against value, or of every arm value with the input's reference value. `ratio_at_least` uses the ratio of means `mean(arm) / mean(against)` for `higher_better` and `mean(against) / mean(arm)` for `lower_better`. - Missing values, per decision unit: `n_missing` counts the arm's missing values and, against an arm, the against arm's (for `pooled_mean` a replicate counts once; for agreement a pair with a missing side counts once). With `"void"`, any missing value makes the unit void with reason `"missing_values"`. With `"fail"`, a missing value of `arm` makes the unit `"not_supported"` with reason `"missing_values"`, and otherwise a missing value of `against` makes it void with reason `"missing_values"`. - Eligibility (`given`): for each listed comparison, its outcome for this unit is that comparison's row for the same input when both comparisons are decided per input, and otherwise that comparison's outcome, where `"per_input"` counts as supported only when every row is. When any of these is not `"supported"`, the unit is void with reason `"not_eligible"`. - Interval: for `all_pairs`, `[lo, hi]` is the minimum and maximum of the differences, and needs at least one difference. For `bootstrap`, the ratio of means is recomputed on `bootstrap_resamples` resamples (`B`) with replacement of the unit's paired replicates, drawn from one `random.Random(bootstrap_seed)` stream in comparison order, and `[lo, hi]` is the `(1 - confidence) / 2` and `(1 + confidence) / 2` empirical quantiles (sorted resamples, index `floor(q * (B - 1))`); it needs at least two replicates. `estimate` is the mean difference (`all_pairs`) or the ratio of means (`bootstrap`) on the full data. Too few values gives outcome `"void"` with reason `"insufficient_replicates"`. - Margin value `m`: 0 for a null margin, `x` for `{"abs": x}`. - Outcome per decision unit, in this order: eligibility; then, for agreement, any compared pair that disagrees makes the unit not supported; then the missing-value rule; then the interval's minimum count; then the criterion. The criterion gives `"supported"`, `"not_supported"` or else `"inconclusive"`: agreement is supported when at least one pair was compared, every compared pair agrees and none is missing (with no compared pair, it is void with reason `"missing_values"`); non-inferiority (`higher_better`) is supported when `lo >= -m`, not supported when `hi < -m`; non-inferiority (`lower_better`) is supported when `hi <= m`, not supported when `lo > m`; superiority (`two_sided`) is supported when `lo > m` or `hi < -m`, not supported when `-m <= lo` and `hi <= m`; ratio with `strict` false is supported when `lo >= threshold`, not supported when `hi < threshold`; ratio with `strict` true is supported when `lo > threshold`, not supported when `hi <= threshold`. - `sign` of a unit is `"higher"` when a superiority is supported with `lo > m`, `"lower"` when it is supported with `hi < -m`, and null otherwise. - A comparison's outcome: for `pooled_mean`, its one unit's outcome; for `per_input_all`, supported when every input is supported, not supported when any input is not supported, void when any input is void and none is not supported, otherwise inconclusive; for `per_input_each`, `"per_input"`, with each input's outcome in its rows. - `C/comparison_scored.json`, atomic, is exactly `{comparison_sha256, comparisons, totals}`. `comparisons` follows the design's order, each exactly `{id, arm, against, criterion, unit, outcome, rows}`; `rows` has one row per decision unit (`input` null for `pooled_mean`), each exactly `{input, n, n_missing, estimate, lo, hi, margin_value, threshold, outcome, sign, reason, pairs}`. `n` counts the differences, ratios or compared pairs; `pairs` is null for metric comparisons and, for agreement, the per-replicate rows `{replicate, agrees, missing, max_abs_error, max_rel_error}` (`agrees` null and `missing` true when a side is missing). Numbers are null when void; `reason` is `"missing_values"`, `"insufficient_replicates"` or `"not_eligible"` for a void unit, `"missing_values"` for a unit made not supported by the `"fail"` rule, and null otherwise. `totals` is exactly `{supported, not_supported, inconclusive, void}`, counting decision units over all comparisons. - Exit 0 after writing; exit 1 for invalid or missing input (a design that intake would reject included), a seal mismatch or a failed write, with no output file. A missing or invalid `wrap.json` or fetched file is not invalid input; it is a missing value. Diagnostics contain no input content. A scoring failure fails evaluate with `error_class: parse`. - Evaluate status in comparison mode is PASS once `C/comparison_scored.json` was written, whatever the outcomes. Evaluate facts keep every existing key, null in comparison mode.

1	Can MEGADOCK’s GPU implementation make denser docking search affordable, and does that improve pose recovery within a fixed budget?
2	
3	Use the four unbound PINDER cases examined by blind01’s unit probe. Pin their exact identities, prepared inputs and reference structures before execution. Treat this as a small pilot.
4	
5	Compare three configurations:
6	
7	1. CPU execution with standard rotational sampling.
8	2. GPU execution with the same sampling and scientific settings.
9	3. GPU execution with the documented denser rotational sampling.
10	
11	Use MEGADOCK’s existing implementations. Keep scoring settings and the number of retained predictions fixed at 50.
12	
13	First establish correct execution and scientific agreement between CPU and GPU configurations at identical search settings. Define justified numerical tolerances before examining comparative results.
14	
15	Then measure whether denser search improves recovery. Report DockQ for the top-ranked prediction and the best of 50 separately. Use reference structures only for evaluation.
16	
17	Use a small runtime calibration to define feasible budgets. Seal configurations, timing repetitions, comparison rules and the total spending cap before evaluation. Report complete workflow time, GPU activity and billed allocation cost.
18	
19	Keep three conclusions separate: execution acceleration, scientific agreement at identical settings, and quality changes from additional search. Preserve negative results and budget overruns.
20	
21	Identify any pipeline contract that cannot express these comparisons. Report that limitation explicitly without substituting a different scientific question.
22	
23	Limit conclusions to these four cases. Do not infer biological efficacy from docking accuracy.
24	
25	## Materials from blind-01 records (owner decisions 2026-11-02; recorded by an authorized reader agent)
26	
27	
28	Owner’s answer, 2026-11-02, case identities:

30	> "Codex addendum": a Codex reader copies the four case identities, their prepared input records and reference-structure sources from blind-01's records into a labelled section added to the brief. Your text stays unchanged.

Can MEGADOCK’s GPU implementation make denser docking search affordable, and does that improve pose recovery within a fixed budget?

Use the four unbound PINDER cases examined by blind01’s unit probe. Pin their exact identities, prepared inputs and reference structures before execution. Treat this as a small pilot.

Compare three configurations:

1. CPU execution with standard rotational sampling.
2. GPU execution with the same sampling and scientific settings.
3. GPU execution with the documented denser rotational sampling.

Use MEGADOCK’s existing implementations. Keep scoring settings and the number of retained predictions fixed at 50.

First establish correct execution and scientific agreement between CPU and GPU configurations at identical search settings. Define justified numerical tolerances before examining comparative results.

Then measure whether denser search improves recovery. Report DockQ for the top-ranked prediction and the best of 50 separately. Use reference structures only for evaluation.

Use a small runtime calibration to define feasible budgets. Seal configurations, timing repetitions, comparison rules and the total spending cap before evaluation. Report complete workflow time, GPU activity and billed allocation cost.

Keep three conclusions separate: execution acceleration, scientific agreement at identical settings, and quality changes from additional search. Preserve negative results and budget overruns.

Identify any pipeline contract that cannot express these comparisons. Report that limitation explicitly without substituting a different scientific question.

Limit conclusions to these four cases. Do not infer biological efficacy from docking accuracy.

## Comparison request (science step s32)

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, inputs, outputs, metrics and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is the seed's main comparison on the seed's four cases. Earlier runs of this route recorded the same programs on other inputs; their records are not part of this run. Preserve the seed above.

What the run does

- Three arms, as the view describes them, one for each of the seed's three configurations. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1, MEGADOCK on the CPU with standard rotational sampling). A1 is the seed's configuration 2 (MEGADOCK on the GPU with the same sampling and scientific settings). A2 is the seed's configuration 3 (MEGADOCK on the GPU with the documented denser rotational sampling, MEGADOCK's `-D` option, and every other setting as in A1). Every arm keeps 50 ranked predictions and reconstructs and assembles each of them the same way. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself, with the arm's `env`; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four inputs, as the view describes them: the seed's four unbound (apo) PINDER `2024-02` cases listed in the materials above, `1aua`, `1ax2`, `1dv1` and `1nr5`. Each input's `spec` pins the case: its PINDER system, the canonical apo receptor and ligand sources (name, URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, the SHA-256 of each prepared file, the native complex, which only the evaluator may read, and the OpenMP thread count of the arms.
- SHA-256 form in the view: in every input's `spec`, each SHA-256 (`receptor_source.sha256`, `ligand_source.sha256`, `prepared_sha256.receptor`, `prepared_sha256.ligand`, `reference.sha256`) is an array of lowercase hexadecimal strings, as the spec's `sha256_form` states. The digest is the concatenation of the array's strings in order, a 64-character lowercase hexadecimal string; every script that checks or records a digest uses that concatenation. The source and reference digests are also listed, whole, in the materials above.
- Thread count: each arm's `env` sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to the spec's `omp_threads.tens` followed by `omp_threads.ones` (two one-character strings, the same in every input), which the pipeline substitutes before it runs the arm. No adapter or harness script sets, reads or changes it.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.
- Metrics, as the view describes them: the trusted wall of each invocation, measured by the pipeline; and, read from the evaluator's `dockq.json` by the extraction rules below, the DockQ of the top-ranked model and the largest DockQ over the 50 models.

Which harness files reach the box

- The pipeline uploads only these files from `harness/` to the box: `setup.sh`, `run_anchors.sh`, `run_command.sh`; `run_evaluation.sh`, `run_units.sh` and `units.json` when they exist; and the sealed comparison files `arms/<arm id>.sh`, `cmp_files.json`, `cmp_extract.json`, `versions.sh`, `fetch_private.sh` and `evaluate.sh`. Any other file written under `harness/` (a Python helper, a JSON list of inputs, a table of published values) never reaches the box. A repair may change only `setup.sh` (or `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh`); the sealed comparison files are never repaired, so a defect in one of them stops the run.
- Every one of these scripts is therefore self-contained: it reads no file under `harness/` except itself, and carries in its own text every list, value and program it needs, or reads it from the variables the pipeline sets (`CMP_INPUT`, `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`, `CMP_OUT`, `CMP_ARM_OUT`, `CMP_EVAL_OUT`, `CMP_PRIVATE`). Write no other file under `harness/`.
- `fetch_private.sh` runs as a separate user with the private directory as its working directory and has no `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; its output is not kept. It carries in its own text, for each of the four inputs, the native complex's name, URL, byte count and SHA-256 (the concatenated digest of `spec.reference.sha256`) exactly as `spec.reference` gives them in the view, downloads each one, checks its byte count and SHA-256 (a mismatch exits nonzero), and writes it under its working directory at that name.
- `evaluate.sh` takes the input id from `CMP_INPUT` and the native complex's name, byte count and SHA-256 (the concatenation of the pieces) from `spec.reference` in `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; it reads no input list from any file.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. A1 and A2 use the same `megadock-gpu` executable. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Seed inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec` (for `1aua`, `1ax2` and `1nr5` the receptor and ligand come from the same apo file), checks the byte count and the SHA-256 recorded there (the concatenated digest; any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the one-character chain identifier field of the PDB format (chainID) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. It then checks the SHA-256 of every prepared file against the concatenated digest of the input's `spec.prepared_sha256` (any mismatch stops the run) and records them in its setup record. The URLs, byte counts, SHA-256 digests and prepared paths are written in `setup.sh` itself. Neither the PINDER index nor the test-monomer archive is needed.
- Native complexes: only `fetch_private.sh` fetches them, from the URLs in the inputs' `spec.reference`, and checks their byte counts and SHA-256. `setup.sh`, the adapters and the arms never fetch, copy or read them.
- Evaluator: install PINDER from the pinned source archive (URL and SHA-256 in the materials above and in the view), as run9's excerpt above shows, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. After installing it, `setup.sh` checks that the evaluator's interpreter imports `BiotiteDockQ` from `pinder.eval.dockq` (an import only; no private data, no scoring) and stops setup if it does not. `evaluate.sh` reads `model_<rank>.pdb` from `CMP_ARM_OUT` in rank order, scores each against the input's native complex under `CMP_PRIVATE` with BiotiteDockQ and the model's chains `R` and `L` mapped to the native's receptor and ligand chains, and writes `CMP_EVAL_OUT/dockq.json` as one JSON array of the DockQ values in rank order with no other number. Per-model components, if written, go to a separate file.
- Evaluator invocation: BiotiteDockQ is constructed with `parallel_io=False`, so it reads the models in its own process. PINDER's parallel reader starts worker processes with the `spawn` method, which re-imports the main program from its file; a program given to Python on standard input has no such file, and the workers then fail and the pool never returns. `evaluate.sh` carries the evaluator's Python program in its own text (for example in a quoted here-document written with `cat`), writes it at each call to a regular file under `CMP_EVAL_OUT` (for example under `CMP_EVAL_OUT/tmp/`), and runs it as `"$VPY" <that file>`. It never runs `python -` with a here-document or any other standard-input program, and never runs a Python file kept under `harness/`, which is not on the box.
- `cmp_files.json`: for each of A0, A1 and A2, `transforms` and `scores` at `out/docking.out`; `coords` at `{"glob": "out/model_*.pdb"}`; `dockq` at `eval/dockq.json`.
- `cmp_extract.json`: for each of A0, A1 and A2, one rule for `dockq_rank1` and one for `dockq_best50`, each `{"file": "eval/dockq.json", "kind": "json", "expr": ""}` (the empty JSON Pointer, the whole array); the pipeline reduces the array as each metric states.
- `versions.sh`: for A0 the `megadock` executable, for A1 and A2 the `megadock-gpu` executable, and for the evaluator the Python interpreter that runs it, each with its version string (the MEGADOCK commit for the MEGADOCK arms, the installed PINDER version for the evaluator).
- Reproduce for A0: no published anchors exist for these inputs. `run_anchors.sh` writes `out/anchors_measured.json` as `{}`, as earlier runs of this route did. `run_command.sh` may run A0's two commands once on input `1aua` as a smoke check of the build, with A0's `env` values as the view gives them after substitution; it compares and evaluates nothing.

Boundaries

- No agent, adapter or harness script computes, prints or asserts any difference between arms, any tolerance or any summary of DockQ values. The pipeline records and compares the outputs.
- Reference structures are used only by the evaluator.
- Preserve every invocation's files, failures and timeouts as they are. Do not rerun any invocation outside the pipeline's schedule.
- If intake or the harness cannot express this run within these boundaries, report the exact contract gap and stop before paid work.

## Comparison request (science step s32)

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, inputs, outputs, metrics and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is the seed's main comparison on the seed's four cases. Earlier runs of this route recorded the same programs on other inputs; their records are not part of this run. Preserve the seed above.

What the run does

- Three arms, as the view describes them, one for each of the seed's three configurations. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1, MEGADOCK on the CPU with standard rotational sampling). A1 is the seed's configuration 2 (MEGADOCK on the GPU with the same sampling and scientific settings). A2 is the seed's configuration 3 (MEGADOCK on the GPU with the documented denser rotational sampling, MEGADOCK's `-D` option, and every other setting as in A1). Every arm keeps 50 ranked predictions and reconstructs and assembles each of them the same way. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself, with the arm's `env`; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four inputs, as the view describes them: the seed's four unbound (apo) PINDER `2024-02` cases listed in the materials above, `1aua`, `1ax2`, `1dv1` and `1nr5`. Each input's `spec` pins the case: its PINDER system, the canonical apo receptor and ligand sources (name, URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, the SHA-256 of each prepared file, the native complex, which only the evaluator may read, and the OpenMP thread count of the arms.
- SHA-256 form in the view: in every input's `spec`, each SHA-256 (`receptor_source.sha256`, `ligand_source.sha256`, `prepared_sha256.receptor`, `prepared_sha256.ligand`, `reference.sha256`) is an array of lowercase hexadecimal strings, as the spec's `sha256_form` states. The digest is the concatenation of the array's strings in order, a 64-character lowercase hexadecimal string; every script that checks or records a digest uses that concatenation. The source and reference digests are also listed, whole, in the materials above.
- Thread count: each arm's `env` sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to the spec's `omp_threads.tens` followed by `omp_threads.ones` (two one-character strings, the same in every input), which the pipeline substitutes before it runs the arm's commands. No adapter sets, reads or changes it.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.
- Metrics, as the view describes them: the trusted wall of each invocation, measured by the pipeline; and, read from the evaluator's `dockq.json` by the extraction rules below, the DockQ of the top-ranked model and the largest DockQ over the 50 models.

Which harness files reach the box

- The pipeline uploads only these files from `harness/` to the box: `setup.sh`, `run_anchors.sh`, `run_command.sh`; `run_evaluation.sh`, `run_units.sh` and `units.json` when they exist; and the sealed comparison files `arms/<arm id>.sh`, `cmp_files.json`, `cmp_extract.json`, `versions.sh`, `fetch_private.sh` and `evaluate.sh`. Any other file written under `harness/` (a Python helper, a JSON list of inputs, a table of published values) never reaches the box. A repair may change only `setup.sh` (or `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh`); the sealed comparison files are never repaired, so a defect in one of them stops the run.
- Every one of these scripts is therefore self-contained: it reads no file under `harness/` except itself, and carries in its own text every list, value and program it needs, or reads it from the variables the pipeline sets (`CMP_INPUT`, `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`, `CMP_OUT`, `CMP_ARM_OUT`, `CMP_EVAL_OUT`, `CMP_PRIVATE`). Write no other file under `harness/`.
- `fetch_private.sh` runs as a separate user with the private directory as its working directory and has no `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; its output is not kept. It carries in its own text, for each of the four inputs, the native complex's name, URL, byte count and SHA-256 (the concatenated digest of `spec.reference.sha256`) exactly as `spec.reference` gives them in the view, downloads each one, checks its byte count and SHA-256 (a mismatch exits nonzero), and writes it under its working directory at that name.
- `evaluate.sh` takes the input id from `CMP_INPUT` and the native complex's name, byte count and SHA-256 (the concatenation of the pieces) from `spec.reference` in `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; it reads no input list from any file.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. A1 and A2 use the same `megadock-gpu` executable. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Seed inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec` (for `1aua`, `1ax2` and `1nr5` the receptor and ligand come from the same apo file), checks the byte count and the SHA-256 recorded there (the concatenated digest; any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the one-character chain identifier field of the PDB format (chainID) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. It then checks the SHA-256 of every prepared file against the concatenated digest of the input's `spec.prepared_sha256` (any mismatch stops the run) and records them in its setup record. The URLs, byte counts, SHA-256 digests and prepared paths are written in `setup.sh` itself. Neither the PINDER index nor the test-monomer archive is needed.
- Native complexes: only `fetch_private.sh` fetches them, from the URLs in the inputs' `spec.reference`, and checks their byte counts and SHA-256. `setup.sh`, the adapters and the arms never fetch, copy or read them.
- Evaluator: install PINDER from the pinned source archive (URL and SHA-256 in the materials above and in the view), as run9's excerpt above shows, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. After installing it, `setup.sh` checks that the evaluator's interpreter imports `BiotiteDockQ` from `pinder.eval.dockq` (an import only; no private data, no scoring) and stops setup if it does not. `evaluate.sh` reads `model_<rank>.pdb` from `CMP_ARM_OUT` in rank order, scores each against the input's native complex under `CMP_PRIVATE` with BiotiteDockQ and the model's chains `R` and `L` mapped to the native's receptor and ligand chains, and writes `CMP_EVAL_OUT/dockq.json` as one JSON array of the DockQ values in rank order with no other number. Per-model components, if written, go to a separate file.
- Evaluator invocation: BiotiteDockQ is constructed with `parallel_io=False`, so it reads the models in its own process. PINDER's parallel reader starts worker processes with the `spawn` method, which re-imports the main program from its file; a program given to Python on standard input has no such file, and the workers then fail and the pool never returns. `evaluate.sh` carries the evaluator's Python program in its own text (for example in a quoted here-document written with `cat`), writes it at each call to a regular file under `CMP_EVAL_OUT` (for example under `CMP_EVAL_OUT/tmp/`), and runs it as `"$VPY" <that file>`. It never runs `python -` with a here-document or any other standard-input program, and never runs a Python file kept under `harness/`, which is not on the box.
- `cmp_files.json`: for each of A0, A1 and A2, `transforms` and `scores` at `out/docking.out`; `coords` at `{"glob": "out/model_*.pdb"}`; `dockq` at `eval/dockq.json`.
- `cmp_extract.json`: for each of A0, A1 and A2, one rule for `dockq_rank1` and one for `dockq_best50`, each `{"file": "eval/dockq.json", "kind": "json", "expr": ""}` (the empty JSON Pointer, the whole array); the pipeline reduces the array as each metric states.
- `versions.sh`: for A0 the `megadock` executable, for A1 and A2 the `megadock-gpu` executable, and for the evaluator the Python interpreter that runs it, each with its version string (the MEGADOCK commit for the MEGADOCK arms, the installed PINDER version for the evaluator).
- Reproduce for A0: no published anchors exist for these inputs. `run_anchors.sh` writes `out/anchors_measured.json` as `{}`, as earlier runs of this route did. `run_command.sh` may run A0's two commands once on input `1aua` as a smoke check of the build; it compares and evaluates nothing.

Boundaries

- No agent, adapter or harness script computes, prints or asserts any difference between arms, any tolerance or any summary of DockQ values. The pipeline records and compares the outputs.
- Reference structures are used only by the evaluator.
- Preserve every invocation's files, failures and timeouts as they are. Do not rerun any invocation outside the pipeline's schedule.
- If intake or the harness cannot express this run within these boundaries, report the exact contract gap and stop before paid work.

Can MEGADOCK’s GPU implementation make denser docking search affordable, and does that improve pose recovery within a fixed budget?

Use the four unbound PINDER cases examined by blind01’s unit probe. Pin their exact identities, prepared inputs and reference structures before execution. Treat this as a small pilot.

Compare three configurations:

1. CPU execution with standard rotational sampling.
2. GPU execution with the same sampling and scientific settings.

## Comparison request (science step s32)

This request asks for one comparison-mode run: the arms, inputs, outputs, metrics and evaluator exactly as the comparison view (`comparison_view.json`) describes them. It is the seed's main comparison on the seed's four cases. Earlier runs of this route recorded the same programs on other inputs; their records are not part of this run. Preserve the seed above.

What the run does

- Three arms, as the view describes them, one for each of the seed's three configurations. A0 is the published baseline (the seed's configuration 1, MEGADOCK on the CPU with standard rotational sampling). A1 is the seed's configuration 2 (MEGADOCK on the GPU with the same sampling and scientific settings). A2 is the seed's configuration 3 (MEGADOCK on the GPU with the documented denser rotational sampling, MEGADOCK's `-D` option, and every other setting as in A1). Every arm keeps 50 ranked predictions and reconstructs and assembles each of them the same way. The pipeline runs every arm's commands itself, with the arm's `env`; the adapters only check that the input's prepared files exist.
- Four inputs, as the view describes them: the seed's four unbound (apo) PINDER `2024-02` cases listed in the materials above, `1aua`, `1ax2`, `1dv1` and `1nr5`. Each input's `spec` pins the case: its PINDER system, the canonical apo receptor and ligand sources (name, URL, byte count, SHA-256), the prepared paths the arms read, the SHA-256 of each prepared file, the native complex, which only the evaluator may read, and the OpenMP thread count of the arms.
- SHA-256 form in the view: in every input's `spec`, each SHA-256 (`receptor_source.sha256`, `ligand_source.sha256`, `prepared_sha256.receptor`, `prepared_sha256.ligand`, `reference.sha256`) is an array of lowercase hexadecimal strings, as the spec's `sha256_form` states. The digest is the concatenation of the array's strings in order, a 64-character lowercase hexadecimal string; every script that checks or records a digest uses that concatenation. The source and reference digests are also listed, whole, in the materials above.
- Thread count: each arm's `env` sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS` to the spec's `omp_threads.tens` followed by `omp_threads.ones` (two one-character strings, the same in every input), which the pipeline substitutes before it runs the arm's commands. No adapter sets, reads or changes it.
- The evaluator: PINDER's DockQ implementation at the pinned commit, as the view describes it, scoring each arm's assembled models of one input against that input's native complex.
- Outputs, as the view describes them: the ranked rows of each arm's `docking.out` (transform fields and score field), the coordinates of the assembled models, and the evaluator's DockQ value for each model. They are recorded and compared across arms by the pipeline. No agent computes or reports a comparison.
- Metrics, as the view describes them: the trusted wall of each invocation, measured by the pipeline; and, read from the evaluator's `dockq.json` by the extraction rules below, the DockQ of the top-ranked model and the largest DockQ over the 50 models.

Which harness files reach the box

- The pipeline uploads only these files from `harness/` to the box: `setup.sh`, `run_anchors.sh`, `run_command.sh`; `run_evaluation.sh`, `run_units.sh` and `units.json` when they exist; and the sealed comparison files `arms/<arm id>.sh`, `cmp_files.json`, `cmp_extract.json`, `versions.sh`, `fetch_private.sh` and `evaluate.sh`. Any other file written under `harness/` (a Python helper, a JSON list of inputs, a table of published values) never reaches the box. A repair may change only `setup.sh` (or `run_anchors.sh` and `run_command.sh`); the sealed comparison files are never repaired, so a defect in one of them stops the run.
- Every one of these scripts is therefore self-contained: it reads no file under `harness/` except itself, and carries in its own text every list, value and program it needs, or reads it from the variables the pipeline sets (`CMP_INPUT`, `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`, `CMP_OUT`, `CMP_ARM_OUT`, `CMP_EVAL_OUT`, `CMP_PRIVATE`). Write no other file under `harness/`.
- `fetch_private.sh` runs as a separate user with the private directory as its working directory and has no `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; its output is not kept. It carries in its own text, for each of the four inputs, the native complex's name, URL, byte count and SHA-256 (the concatenated digest of `spec.reference.sha256`) exactly as `spec.reference` gives them in the view, downloads each one, checks its byte count and SHA-256 (a mismatch exits nonzero), and writes it under its working directory at that name.
- `evaluate.sh` takes the input id from `CMP_INPUT` and the native complex's name, byte count and SHA-256 (the concatenation of the pieces) from `spec.reference` in `CMP_INPUT_SPEC`; it reads no input list from any file.

Materials, pins and preparation

- MEGADOCK: the published repository https://github.com/akiyamalab/MEGADOCK at commit `9575280c875732553266e26adc607dd892b02616`, built twice from the same checkout under `baseline-published/megadock/` in the shared run directory, so that `baseline-published/megadock/megadock`, `baseline-published/megadock/megadock-gpu` and `baseline-published/megadock/decoygen` exist there. A1 and A2 use the same `megadock-gpu` executable. The CUDA samples headers come from https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples at tag `v12.8`; they are build dependencies only. The CPU build uses single-precision FFTW exactly as below. The GPU build keeps `-Xcompiler -fopenmp` and `-use_fast_math` and the libraries below, and targets the compute capability of the GPU on this box: `setup.sh` reads it with `nvidia-smi --query-gpu=compute_cap --format=csv,noheader` (for example `8.6` gives `sm_86`, `9.0` gives `sm_90`, `8.0` gives `sm_80`), passes that one target as `SM_VERSIONS` and in `-arch`, records it in the setup record, and checks with `cuobjdump --list-elf` (from the CUDA toolkit) that `megadock-gpu` contains code for that target; a missing target stops setup. Historical build commands for an `sm_90` box (blind-02 m5 run2 `setup.sh:52-80`, as carried by earlier briefs of this route; replace `sm_90` by the box's target):

```bash
if [[ ! -d baseline-published/cuda-samples/.git ]]; then
    git clone --depth 1 --branch v12.8 https://github.com/NVIDIA/cuda-samples baseline-published/cuda-samples
fi
git -C baseline-published/cuda-samples describe --tags --exact-match
samples=$(pwd)/baseline-published/cuda-samples
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=0 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ FFTW_INSTALL_PATH=/usr \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include FFTW_LDFLAGS='-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f'
make -C baseline-published/megadock -j 8 USE_GPU=1 USE_MPI=0 \
    CPPCOMPILER=/usr/bin/g++ SM_VERSIONS=sm_90 \
    "NVCC=$CUDA_NVCC -Xcompiler -fopenmp -arch=sm_90 -use_fast_math" \
    "INCLUDES=-Isrc -I$CUDA_INCLUDE -I$samples/Common" \
    FFTW_CFLAGS=-I/usr/include \
    "LIB=-lm -L/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu -lfftw3f -L$CUDA_LIB -Wl,-rpath,$CUDA_LIB -lcudart -lcufft"
```

  CUDA paths are discovered on the box. In this published release `megadock -h` and `megadock-gpu -h` print their usage and exit with status 255; accept that status only together with the usage text.
- Seed inputs: `setup.sh` fetches each input's receptor and ligand source from the URL in its `spec` (for `1aua`, `1ax2` and `1nr5` the receptor and ligand come from the same apo file), checks the byte count and the SHA-256 recorded there (the concatenated digest; any mismatch stops the run), and writes the prepared files to the `spec`'s `prepared` paths under the shared run directory by changing only the one-character chain identifier field of the PDB format (chainID) to `R` in the receptor and `L` in the ligand on ATOM, HETATM, ANISOU and TER records, keeping every other byte and line. It then checks the SHA-256 of every prepared file against the concatenated digest of the input's `spec.prepared_sha256` (any mismatch stops the run) and records them in its setup record. The URLs, byte counts, SHA-256 digests and prepared paths are written in `setup.sh` itself. Neither the PINDER index nor the test-monomer archive is needed.
- Native complexes: only `fetch_private.sh` fetches them, from the URLs in the inputs' `spec.reference`, and checks their byte counts and SHA-256. `setup.sh`, the adapters and the arms never fetch, copy or read them.
- Evaluator: install PINDER from the pinned source archive (URL and SHA-256 in the materials above and in the view), as run9's excerpt above shows, under the shared run directory or with apt, never under the home directory. After installing it, `setup.sh` checks that the evaluator's interpreter imports `BiotiteDockQ` from `pinder.eval.dockq` (an import only; no private data, no scoring) and stops setup if it does not. `evaluate.sh` reads `model_<rank>.pdb` from `CMP_ARM_OUT` in rank order, scores each against the input's native complex under `CMP_PRIVATE` with BiotiteDockQ and the model's chains `R` and `L` mapped to the native's receptor and ligand chains, and writes `CMP_EVAL_OUT/dockq.json` as one JSON array of the DockQ values in rank order with no other number. Per-model components, if written, go to a separate file.
- Evaluator invocation: BiotiteDockQ is constructed with `parallel_io=False`, so it reads the models in its own process. PINDER's parallel reader starts worker processes with the `spawn` method, which re-imports the main program from its file; a program given to Python on standard input has no such file, and the workers then fail and the pool never returns. `evaluate.sh` carries the evaluator's Python program in its own text (for example in a quoted here-document written with `cat`), writes it at each call to a regular file under `CMP_EVAL_OUT` (for example under `CMP_EVAL_OUT/tmp/`), and runs it as `"$VPY" <that file>`. It never runs `python -` with a here-document or any other standard-input program, and never runs a Python file kept under `harness/`, which is not on the box.
- `cmp_files.json`: for each of A0, A1 and A2, `transforms` and `scores` at `out/docking.out`; `coords` at `{"glob": "out/model_*.pdb"}`; `dockq` at `eval/dockq.json`.
- `cmp_extract.json`: for each of A0, A1 and A2, one rule for `dockq_rank1` and one for `dockq_best50`, each `{"file": "eval/dockq.json", "kind": "json", "expr": ""}` (the empty JSON Pointer, the whole array); the pipeline reduces the array as each metric states.
- `versions.sh`: for A0 the `megadock` executable, for A1 and A2 the `megadock-gpu` executable, and for the evaluator the Python interpreter that runs it, each with its version string (the MEGADOCK commit for the MEGADOCK arms, the installed PINDER version for the evaluator).
- Reproduce for A0: no published anchors exist for these inputs. `run_anchors.sh` writes `out/anchors_measured.json` as `{}`, as earlier runs of this route did. `run_command.sh` may run A0's two commands once on input `1aua` as a smoke check of the build; it compares and evaluates nothing.

Boundaries

- No agent, adapter or harness script computes, prints or asserts any difference between arms, any tolerance or any summary of DockQ values. The pipeline records and compares the outputs.
- Reference structures are used only by the evaluator.
- Preserve every invocation's files, failures and timeouts as they are. Do not rerun any invocation outside the pipeline's schedule.
- If intake or the harness cannot express this run within these boundaries, report the exact contract gap and stop before paid work.
